@@119162932 <p> Elon Musk is confident that his company can make humanity an interplanetary civilization by reaching Mars . However , becoming such a civilization involves more than just setting up a habitat on the Red Planet . To thrive , humans would need energy security and that 's something we have n't fully mastered on Earth either . <p> From the early days of working with stone-based tools to now unlocking artificial intelligence ( AI ) , humanity has come a long way . This has been possible due to our ability to tap into various energy sources , starting from firewood to fossil fuels , and more recently , turning a new page by harnessing energy from the winds , sunlight , and other renewable energy sources . <p> But we have n't yet figured out how to tap into all the major energy sources available to us . Only after we do so , would we achieve the status of a Type I or planetary civilization , a necessary stepping stone before becoming interplanetary . <h> What is a Type 1 civilization ? <p> A Type I Civilization is the first of the three types of civilizations that can potentially exist , as per Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev . This three-type classification is based on the amount of energy available to a civilization , which is also a reflection of its technological progress . <p> Kardashev 's classification is based on the simple premise that the more technologically advanced a civilization is , the more energy it can tap into , which in-turn leads to more improvements in its technology . <p> This has been evident in human history as well , where technological advances have led to more ways of harnessing energy , which has then led to further advances in technology . But Kardashev uses the scale to gauge if the civilization is planetary , stellar , or galaxy-spanning . <p> In his view , a Type I or planetary civilization is limited to one planet but has reached the level where it can access all the energy available . A Type II civilization can harness all the energy available from its star and colonize multiple planets in the solar system . <p> A Type III civilization would be able to replicate Type II achievements across multiple stars and planets and truly become intergalactic and set up empires . While this is stuff that makes science-fiction , humanity is not very far from being a Type I civilization . <p> Nearly a decade after Kardashev proposed this classification , American astronomer and planetary scientist Carl Sagan , in 1973 , estimated that humanity was perhaps at 0.7 and closer to being a Type I civilization on a scale of 0 to 1 . Over the years , humans have tapped into various other sources of energy . So how far off are we from being a Type I civilization ? <p> According to the Kardashev scale , a civilization would need to be able to harness 1016 watts of energy to be classified as Type I. Our energy consumption as per globally aggregated data stands at 18.8 terawatts or 1.8 x 1013 watts . So , we are still three orders of magnitude away from reaching the energy levels of a Type 1 civilization . <p> The question arises , how do we get there ? <h> Energy sources we can exploit <p> It is well known that our energy consumption primarily comes from fossil fuels . Coal , oil , and natural gas combine to deliver nearly 80% of energy consumed . The remaining 20% is from a mix of nuclear and renewable energy sources including biofuels . <p> However , given the impact of carbon emissions released by mainly using non-renewable sources of fuel , we need to tap into more carbon-free or low-carbon-emitting alternatives . Even if were to devise effective measures for countering carbon emissions , we are inching closer to exhausting these reserves . <p> Estimates suggest that we only have about 47 years of petroleum left at current consumption levels . Coal reserves around the world are at 1.1 trillion tonnes and could last a little over 130 years but natural gas reserves are also rapidly depleting and could be exhausted in the next 100 years . <p> Fossil fuel reserves are rapidly depleting and could be completely exhausted in the next 100 years . Source : joeshmo/iStock <p> By the turn of this century , the world could come to a grinding halt if alternate sources of energy that meet our energy demand are not commercially available . With fossil fuel reserves completely exhausted , humanity will only have renewable and natural energy resources at its disposal to meet energy requirements . <p> Improvements in wind and solar energy technology , therefore , need to be accelerated not just to improve efficiency but also generate larger outputs to keep up with the growing demand . By the turn of the century , these sources would need to take over the contributions of fossil fuels completely . In addition to already commercialized technologies , humanity would also need to tap into new resources of energy that occur naturally . <p> Geothermal energy has hit the ground running and currently contributes to four gigawatts of energy consumption in the US alone . With enhanced geothermal energy systems , researchers are looking to dig deeper , and even volcanoes and geysers are being considered to generate a reliable source of energy . Estimates suggest that the technology could potentially generate about 2,000 GW of energy around the world . <p> Energy from the waves is another potential source that has remained untapped . Although technology to do so is still in its infancy , the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) estimates that wave energy could produce over 29,500 TWh of energy a year . <p> Put together these two sources could generate 5,300 GW or 5.3 TW of power , filling up our current deficit to reach the Type I civilization classification . However , the impending deficit caused by the exhaustion of fossil fuels needs to be addressed . This is where nuclear fusion could help . <h> Nuclear fusion could prove key <p> Human civilization discovered nuclear fission in 1938 . In the next 20 years , technology was commercialized to enable power generation through fission reactions . On the other hand , the technology surrounding nuclear fusions has been more nascent , with the first net gain experiment conducted in December 2022 . However , the progress has been significant enough to render us at the cusp of commercial energy production . <p> Unlike fission , fusion reaction does not produce long-term radioactive waste nor does it require the processing of heavy elements to begin with . Using deuterium and tritium , isotopes of the smallest element hydrogen as reaction fuel , fusion allows us to extract large amounts of energy . <p> When fuel mass is compared , fusion produces four million times as much energy as fossil fuels . A 1,000 MW power plant would require 2.7 million tonnes of coal every year but can function with just 551 pounds ( 250 kg ) of fuel when using fusion technology . <p> Both deuterium and tritium are required in equal amounts but are a very small part of plasma used to bring about fusion reactions . Deuterium exists in all types of water and can easily sourced from abundant seawater . Estimates suggest that every cubic meter of seawater contains 33 grams of deuterium . <p> Interestingly , tritium is produced during the fusion reaction itself when neutrons react with lithium used in the fusion reactor wall . Since large reserves of lithium have already been found and the element can also be extracted from seawater , both the fuel components of nuclear fusion are available in abundance . <p> More importantly , the reaction produces vast amounts of energy without any carbon emissions and could also help solve problems plaguing human civilization today . Once mastered , nuclear fusion can help us fast-track our journey from a Type I to Type II civilization as well . Startups are already working on using fusion technology for interplanetary travel . <p> Therefore , replicating the reaction occurring in stars is n't just a scientific pursuit but a necessary one . <p> 0COMMENT <p> NEWSLETTER <h> The Blueprint Daily <p> Stay up-to-date on engineering , tech , space , and science news with The Blueprint . <h> ABOUT THE EDITOR <p> Ameya Paleja Ameya is a science writer based in Hyderabad , India . A Molecular Biologist at heart , he traded the micropipette to write about science during the pandemic and does not want to go back . He likes to write about genetics , microbes , technology , and public policy . 
@@119162938 <p> Realta Fusion has received the funding from TitletownTech , a venture capital firm formed by Microsoft and the Green Bay Packers . <p> The company is developing modular , compact , magnetic mirror fusion energy generators to power AI-driven infrastructure and other industrial applications , according to reports . Although , TitletownTech did n't specify the amount it invested in Realta Fusion . <h> Innovative approach to fusion energy <p> Fusion offers a clean and sustainable energy source to reduce emissions from " hard-to-decarbonize " industrial processes . Clean energy is the need of today 's era as 37 billion metric tons is the amount of carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) released annually into the atmosphere from energy combustion ( including flaring ) and industrial processes , accelerating climate change . <p> " At Realta Fusion , we 've developed an innovative approach to fusion energy with a right-sized fusion system design -- compact and scalable to provide efficient and reliable solutions for decarbonizing industrial heat and power , " said the company in a statement . <p> The company claims that its magnetic mirror confines a plasma between two high-field superconducting magnets . The strong magnetic fields cause charged , energetic particles to bounce back and forth , also known as the mirror effect . <h> Zero-carbon energy to be used anywhere in the world <p> Realta Fusion maintains that it 's unlocking the limitless potential of humanity , while addressing the threat of climate change . <p> " We are a cutting-edge fusion energy company revolutionizing the way we decarbonize industrial process heat and electricity . We are developing economic , zero-carbon energy to be used anywhere in the world , for everyone in the world , " added the statement . <p> The basis for Realta 's technology is the Wisconsin High-field Axisymmetric Mirror ( WHAM ) project , which operates as a public-private partnership between the company and UW -- Madison . The WHAM project has received over $10m from the DOE 's ARPA-E ( Advanced Research Projects Agency -- Energy ) programme , along with contributions from the University of Wisconsin , Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation , Commonwealth Fusion Systems , and other partners . <p> The company 's approach uses magnetic mirrors to channel deuterium and tritium into a central chamber where it is heated up to extremely high temperatures . <p> The fuels get so hot they turn to plasma and individual particles smash into one another and fuse , a chemical reaction that produces neutrons , heat , helium and electricity . The materials will react with additional lithium-containing materials to create more tritium , which is refined and fed back into the generator to continue the reaction . The heat and electricity are captured for other uses . The heat can be used as-is or can be converted into additional electricity . <p> Realta Fusion , which raised a successful seed financing round in May 2023 led by Khosla Ventures , is targeting the need to decarbonize industrial process heat and power as the fastest path to full-scale deployment of this technology . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> 0COMMENT <p> NEWSLETTER <h> The Blueprint Daily <p> Stay up-to-date on engineering , tech , space , and science news with The Blueprint . <h> ABOUT THE EDITOR <p> Prabhat Ranjan Mishra Prabhat , an alumnus of the Indian Institute of Mass Communication , is a tech and defense journalist . @@119233457 <h> If you 're dreaming of a white Christmas , keep dreaming <p> Ah , the ' White Christmas ' , that hallmark of festive nostalgia , immortalised by Bing Crosby and romanticised in countless Christmas cards . <p> For many , it conjures images of pristine snow blanketing rooftops , children building snowmen , and sleigh bells jingling . In Ireland , however , dreaming of a White Christmas often feels more like an unlikely event . While they do occur occasionally , they remain rare . <p> The history of white Christmases in Ireland <p> Let 's set the record straight : White Christmases in Ireland are uncommon . Officially , Met ? ireann defines a White Christmas as " a single snowflake observed falling anywhere in Ireland on December 25 " . This minimal definition is telling , as snowfall on Christmas Day in Ireland is a rare phenomenon . <p> Historically , snowy Christmases were more common in the 19th and early 20th centuries when winters were generally colder . Anecdotal records describe heavy snowfalls around Christmas during these earlier periods , creating scenes that seemed tailor-made for holiday cards . The shift away from frequent snowfall began in the mid-20th century as winters became milder . <p> The most notable modern White Christmas occurred in 2010 -- a year remembered for its severe and prolonged cold . December 2010 was Ireland 's coldest on record , with consistent subzero temperatures and widespread snow cover . The entire country was blanketed in white , creating a festive tableau that seemed almost too perfect to be real . Transport ground to a halt , and heating systems struggled to cope , but the picturesque landscape softened these inconveniences in the public memory . <p> A frozen over Lough in Cork in January 1987 <p> Previous to that , 1982 marked a notable snowy Christmas . Snow covered much of the country , and icy conditions persisted for days . Earlier still , the Christmas of 1963 is remembered fondly by many for its frosty charm and heavy snowfalls . These events , though rare , stand out in the collective memory as exceptional . <p> Climate change and the melting dream <p> The odds of a White Christmas in Ireland were never great , but climate change is making them even less likely . <p> Winters in Ireland are becoming milder and wetter , with snow increasingly giving way to rain . The shift can be attributed to the accumulation of greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) and methane ( CH4 ) , which trap heat in the Earth 's atmosphere and disrupt historical weather patterns . <p> According to Met ? ireann , the average temperature in Ireland has increased by approximately 1.2 ? C since 1900 . The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) reports that this warming trend is consistent with global patterns , where winter snow cover is shrinking due to higher temperatures . In Ireland , fewer frost days mean a diminished likelihood of snow . Precipitation , while still frequent , increasingly falls as rain rather than snow . <p> Climate models project that Ireland 's winters will continue to warm , with more extreme weather events , including storms and heavy rainfall , becoming the norm . <p> This has cascading effects on ecosystems and human activities . For example , snow-dependent species in Ireland , though limited , could lose vital habitats , and agriculture could face disruptions as milder winters alter growing seasons and increase pest prevalence . <p> The science of snowfall <p> Snow forms when water vapor in the atmosphere condenses into ice crystals , a process requiring cold air temperatures both at the surface and in the upper atmosphere . <p> For snow to fall and accumulate , ground temperatures must remain near or below freezing . In Ireland , these conditions are increasingly rare . Even when cold air masses from the Arctic sweep south , they often collide with warmer , moisture-laden Atlantic systems , producing rain instead of snow . <p> The Gulf Stream , a powerful ocean current , also plays a critical role in shaping Ireland 's winter weather . By transporting warm water from the tropics , it moderates Ireland 's climate , making prolonged cold snaps and heavy snow less likely compared to continental Europe . <p> However , disruptions to the Gulf Stream due to melting Arctic ice and Greenland 's ice sheet could paradoxically increase short-term winter extremes , including occasional heavy snowfalls , even as overall temperatures rise . <p> Betting on snow : A quirky obsession <p> View of Cork City after an overnight snowfall in January 2021 . Picture : Larry Cummins <p> Despite the low probability of a White Christmas , Ireland 's fascination with the idea persists , and the bookmakers love it . Each year , major betting firms roll out odds on whether snow will fall on December 25 . <p> The definition varies by location : Dublin Airport often serves as the official weather station for determining a White Christmas . Odds typically range from 6/1 to 16/1 , depending on early winter forecasts . These bets might be fun , but they 're rarely a winning gamble ; the actual probability of snow is less than 10% most years . <p> Interestingly , some bookmakers even report spikes in betting activity during particularly cold Decembers , with punters fuelled by optimism rather than meteorological evidence . In 2010 , when Ireland experienced widespread snow , bookies reportedly paid out millions to lucky winners . Such events are rare , however , and most years , the bookmakers come out on top . <p> While the dream of a naturally White Christmas fades , the focus shifts to creating memorable experiences regardless of the weather . This Christmas , whether under clouds , rain , or the rare flurry of snow , Ireland 's celebrations will go on . And for those betting on snow ? Well , there 's always next year . 
@@119233998 <p> On the edge of the Arctic Circle , scientists pulled a whole baby mammoth from the Siberian permafrost . It is only one of seven in the world . <p> Last summer , Russian scientists made an astonishing discovery in the Yakutia , a region making headlines due to the stunningly well-preserved carcasses found lurking in the ice in recent years . <p> Though all the animals recovered were significant in their own right , this time they recovered a baby mammoth remarkably frozen in time for 50,000 years . There are only six whole carcasses that exist in the world . <p> As a researcher involved with the investigation said , the " unique discovery , " gives science a rare snapshot of the entire animal . The head and trunk hardly ever survive the hungry animal kingdom once the animal begins to thaw out . <h> Meet Yana , one of the only whole baby mammoths ever found on Earth <p> Nicknamed Yana , the baby mammoth was recently shown at the North-Eastern Federal University at Yakutsk . <p> " We were all surprised by the exceptional preservation of the mammoth , " said the university rector , Anatoly Nikolayev , via The Guardian . <p> In a remarkable state of preservation , Yana managed to keep her trunk and head for 50,000 years . <p> Maxim Cherpasov , the head of Lazarev Mammoth Museum Laboratory in Yakutsk , told Reuters why that was so unusual . And it was quite an interesting twist of fate . <p> " As a rule , the part that thaws out first , especially the trunk , is often eaten by modern predators or birds . Here , for example , even though the forelimbs have already been eaten , the head is remarkably well preserved . " <p> The small-looking elephant came from a natural phenomenon known as the Batagaika crater , which climate change helped to form . Found frozen in time , Yana from a massive depression more than 260 feet deep that kept widening due to the environmental shift , as per the Guardian . <p> At 4 feet , she was removed from her icy grave on an improvised stretcher , as she also weighed a hefty 240-397 pounds . Scientists could estimate that she was a little over a year old when she died though they have not conducted tests to confirm her age as of yet . <h> The Yakutia : A giant freezer making headlines <p> The Yakutia region , a remote location bordering the Arctic Ocean , has extremely freezing temperatures that can drop to -60 degrees Celcius or -95 degrees Fahrenheit . It is the coldest part of Russia . <h> RECOMMENDED ARTICLES <p> Recently , this region has been popping up in news headlines due to the magnificent carcasses from the Earth 's distant past that it holds . Thus far , scientists have acquired a horse , bison , and lemming , The Guardian reports . <p> Most notably , the Arctic wonder has produced a 44,000-year-old wolf carcass , possibly with microbes , even , and a 32,000 saber-toothed cat cub , Reuters adds . <p> As Yana has risen from the depths , she has now joined an illustrious rank of mammoths whose bodies are whole . Only several in the world hold such a prestigious position , and what might Yana , just a babe when she perished , have to teach scientists ? <p> 0COMMENT <p> NEWSLETTER <h> The Blueprint Daily <p> Stay up-to-date on engineering , tech , space , and science news with The Blueprint . <h> ABOUT THE EDITOR <p> Maria Mocerino Originally from LA , Maria Mocerino has been published in Business Insider , The Irish Examiner , The Rogue Mag , Chacruna Institute for Psychedelic Plant Medicines , and now Interesting Engineering .

To read our subscriber-only content . please subscribe or use the reader loyalty code . <h> The Irish Farmers Journal got the opinions of five leading actors in the forestry sector about what could be done to reboot the industry . <p> Ireland will plant around 1,800ha of new forests this year - or less than 25% of the annual national afforestation target of 8,000ha . <p> The Irish Farmers Journal asked five leading actors in the forestry sector to choose three actions which they believe could help reboot the industry and help it navigate an escape from the current malaise . <p> Padraig Egan - SWS Forestry Services <p> Padraig Egan of SWS Forestry Services . <p> " I am a forester involved in private forestry since I came out of college in 1984 . I have been part of taking Ireland 's forest estate from 4% of the country 's land area up to its present 11% , thanks to the ' can-do attitude ' of the various leaders involved down the years , " said Padraig Egan of SWS Forestry Services . <p> " Unfortunately , however , the industry is on its knees today due to the lack and almost total absence of this ' can-do attitude ' , " he maintained . <p> " Yes , we still have some great people working with our forest service , but the forestry sector needs real leadership and a clear focus on what it is trying to achieve . <p> " We had such a focus in previous decades . Only for the pioneers of the past , we would not have one of the best sawmilling sectors in the world , creating much-needed employment in rural Ireland and reducing our dependence on imported materials , " Egan said . <p> " The present forestry programme and its failure to ignite the interest of our farmers and landowners speaks for itself , " he pointed out . <p> Three actions which Egan suggested " could help in moving the dial a little " on planting levels are : <p> 1 . Time lines <p> " An afforestation approval or license can currently take anything from six to 24 months to be sanctioned . This is totally unacceptable to all landowners , whether they be private or investors . Full and final approval or rejection of a forestry application has to be delivered within six months at the outside . And far better consultation is needed between all the various stakeholders in the project -- and that includes the ecologists , " he said . <p> 2 . High nature value farmland <p> " The majority of the productive forestry land on Ireland 's western seaboard is regarded as high nature value farmland ( HNVF ) , thus making it a challenge to get a commercial timber crop approved on it . If some project has a rich resource of HNVF , then the Government should pay an ecological grant and premium to the landowner to protect and manage this ground , while allowing him or her to afforest the remainder of the holding , " Egan suggested . <p> 3 . Promotion <p> " The new forestry programme needs to be vigorously promoted to counter the negative perception of forestry that has taken hold among landowners and farmers . Forestry professionals should be out in farmyards , marts and homesteads promoting forestry to the people that matter . Unfortunately , due to the lack of capacity and financial constraints this is no longer happening within the industry , " he said . <p> Padraig Stapleton - IFA forestry chair <p> Padraig Stapleton of the IFA . <p> Irish Farmers ' Association ( IFA ) farm forestry chair Padraig Stapleton said that the decision of farmers to plant or not will be critical to driving the new planting programme , given that agricultural land accounts for 67% of Ireland 's total land area . The following changes are needed , he maintained , to reboot planting : <p> 1 . Reduce regulatory burden <p> " Substantive concerns remain with regards to excessive regulatory burden that is reducing the viability of forestry on farms . The reality is that many farmers no longer view forestry as a safe investment . The risks associated with committing their land in perpetuity have become too great , " Stapleton said . <p> 2 . Amend payment ecosystem service conditions <p> " The payment ecosystem service ( PES ) payment under the new programme requires farmers to further erode productive area to qualify for payment . This is unacceptable and needs to be amended . Farmers should be paid to manage the land they are required to provide as areas biodiversity enhancement , broadleaves and environmental requirements . They should not be required to further erode productive area to qualify for a payment . The PES rate should reflect the income foregone from timber production and must be extended beyond the seven years payment as there is no financial reward for the successor of the land thereafter , " he argued . <p> 3 . Derisk investment in forestry <p> " New measures are needed to reverse the decline in afforestation , to derisk the investment and restore confidence , while ensuring a balanced regional spread of forestry is achieved , " Stapleton said . " Forestry is no longer guaranteed a safe investment unless there are adequate crisis financial supports put in place by the Government . With the threat of pest and disease looming over the sector , farmers can not absorb the cost of plantations being further destroyed without significant Government support , " Stapleton warned . <p> Teige Ryan - None-So-Hardy Nurseries <p> Teige Ryan of None-So-Hardy . <p> Teige Ryan of None-So-Hardy Nurseries cited timelines and targets , forestry promotion and the establishment of a new forestry development agency as the three measures he believes are vital in restoring confidence in the Irish forestry sector . <p> 1 . Real commitment to licence timelines and targets <p> " While some foresters report noticeable improvements in the speed of applications converting to licences , the weekly Department of Agriculture dashboard still shows little sign of consistency , " Teige Ryan pointed out . <p> " In order to build some level of confidence in the forestry licencing system , the Department must publish their timelines of six to nine months on licences and define the level of service an applicant should expect , " he said . <p> " A forestry licencing plan for 2025 should also be made available outlining the Department 's intentions for the coming year , " he added . <p> 2 . Promotion and marketing of schemes <p> " Professional foresters must be engaged to promote and market all forestry schemes . We need to get better , get out there and communicate the scheme 's benefits to people in a way they will understand so they will see the economic benefits , " Ryan maintained . <p> " Only the expert professional foresters can restore confidence by providing accurate reliable information and combat misinformation , " he said . <p> " In parallel to this , the Department should engage a professional marketing company to develop a three-year strategy at national level , " Ryan suggested . <p> 3 . Establishment of forestry development agency <p> " The creation of a forestry development agency has total support from the forestry industry and needs to be supported by the incoming government , " Teige Ryan claimed . <p> " The establishment of an independent agency would optimise the performance of the Irish forest sector by providing dynamic leadership . Such an agency could proactively engage with the European Commission on a regular basis , could promote the benefits of forestry , counteract negativity , identify and address labour shortages , and ensure targets are reached , " he said . <p> John Roche - Arbor Forest Management <p> John Roche of Arbor Forest Management . <p> John Roche of Arbor Forest Management had three wishes for the forest industry in 2025 : <p> 1 . Approvals <p> " We need to make it easier to get land approved for afforestation . The current scheme is not working and makes it impossible for us to reach the annual target of 8,000ha a year . For example , if a field has more than 30cm of peaty soil , we can not drain it and plant it with conifers . Many fields like this are being farmed , with slurry , fertiliser and chemicals being applied . This type of land was the foundation of previous planting programmes and has produced some of the best forests in the country . If it remains excluded , planting rates will continue to decline , " Roche said . <p> 2 . Imports <p> " The recently announced temporary suspension of the importation of logs from Scotland must be maintained . There are beetle species present in the UK which we must do everything in our power to keep out of Ireland . We need to learn the lessons from the ash dieback disaster , " he maintained . <p> 3 . Forestry development agency <p> " We need a forestry development agency to promote the sector . Forestry has huge potential for rural employment , climate change mitigation and agricultural diversification . Current structures are not working , as evidenced by the low take-up of afforestation . We need a new and innovative approach that incentivises landowners to get involved in forestry , while removing the barriers to planting , harvesting and forest road construction that currently exist , " he said . <p> Olive Leavy - Irish Forest Owners <p> Olive Leavy of Irish Forest Owners . <p> Olive Leavy of the Irish Forest Owners ( IFO ) called for the following changes to how the forestry sector is managed : <p> 1 . Simplify the system <p> " The introduction of a single forest management licence , applicable indefinitely , could significantly reduce unnecessary paperwork . Similarly , a more streamlined afforestation licensing process , without a cost to landowners , would further alleviate barriers , " Leavy said . " Rather than promoting growth and sustainability , the excessive bureaucracy which is currently in place is discouraging farmers , landowners , contractors , foresters and new entrants from participating in the sector , " she maintained . <p> 2 . Remove barriers and adopt owner-focused approach <p> " Key barriers , such as the compulsory planting of broadleaves regardless of site suitability and the replanting obligation , should be removed . The reality is that most forest owners who have planted are unlikely to revert their land back to crops or grazing . The necessity of the replanting obligation , therefore , warrants reconsideration , " Leavy said . " A shift from the current top-down management approach to one that prioritises the needs and goals of forest owners would be transformative , aligning with the motto : ' The right tree , in the right place , for the right reason , with the right management ' , " she claimed . " Afforestation should be guided by the long-term objectives of the landowner ( the right reason ) , ensuring that the chosen tree species and forest type both align with these goals and thrive on the specific site . Central to this approach is the establishment of an education programme for forest owners that starts before planting , focusing on the strengths and limitations of all forest types and management approaches , " Leavy said . <p> 3 . Establish a forestry development agency <p> An independent forestry development agency is essential to supporting Ireland 's forestry sector . This agency could enhance existing markets , explore opportunities for diverse forest products , and promote the benefits of forests to individuals , the economy and the environment , she said . <p> 2024 has been another very disappointing year for Irish forestry . <p> Ireland will plant around 1,800ha of new forests this year - or less than 25% of the annual national afforestation target of 8,000ha . <p> The Irish Farmers Journal asked five leading actors in the forestry sector to choose three actions which they believe could help reboot the industry and help it navigate an escape from the current malaise . <p> Padraig Egan - SWS Forestry Services <p> Padraig Egan of SWS Forestry Services . <p> " I am a forester involved in private forestry since I came out of college in 1984 . @@119252129 <p> As 2024 comes to an end , we 're taking a look at some of the biggest issues shaping our world -- as part of the Whole Hog End of Year Special . <p> So , we shot the messengers . The Greens have been dumped unceremoniously from government in Ireland . But it does n't change the message . Climate change is happening . How we respond is shaping the future , for our descendants and theirs , for centuries . The outlook is grim . <p> The evidence is everywhere -- from the side of 12 misty mountains to the middle of seven sad forests and a dozen dead oceans , the hard rain 's already fallin ' ... Look at your news feed . Monstrous and deadly floods in Valentia , Spain . In Central Europe . In Central Asia , East Africa , South East Asia and the Philippines ... <p> In New England last August , 37.67cm of rain fell in 24 hours . Unprecedented , but let nobody tell you it was an outlier . Heat records were broken this year in Southeast Asia , Africa , North America and Europe . We had the hottest summer on record in the Northern Hemisphere and the warmest winter in the Southern Hemisphere . July 21 , 2024 was the hottest day ever recorded . There were myriad strange weather phenomena . An increase in atmospheric rivers . Melting glaciers . More moisture in the atmosphere , but less water to go ' round . <p> The result ? Famines , wars and migration . <p> The Gulf Stream that keeps us warmer than we should be and is a fundamental , and irreplaceable part of the global ocean circulation system , is failing rapidly . We 'll soon be the new Labrador . And yet , the clear evidence notwithstanding , climate change denial is rampant and there 's well-funded , pushback even against the idea that it 's real . <h> Advertisement <p> There are ( at least ) three strands of opposition : farmers , populists and science deniers , the latter group often supported in many ways by fossil fuel interests . They include the incoming President of the US . As a result , every green centimetre must be won the hard way . And that 's before we factor in the almost incalculable quantities of methane emitted in oil and gas production around the world . <p> Crisis fatigue is another challenge . There 's a bone-weariness out there , with the debate , the tone , the hectoring and moral superiority , understandable as these might be , given the urgency of the issue . Hence the electoral wipeout of the Greens . <p> Climate change has also been sucked into the culture wars . People are fed up . They have lives to live and bills to pay . Our Government 's tendency to pass key development measures over to executive agencies does n't help . Farmers feel they 've a right to be annoyed -- that they 've been unfairly scapegoated . They have a point . <p> They 've been targeted for cuts and exclusions , without any serious attempt being made to find technological or agricultural adaptations . Is there any hope or are we totally screwed ? Both , perhaps . Look at the global fossil fuel emitters , think of Trump , and weep . <p> But let 's not write off the huge positive changes already made , nor the vast body of research-based new technologies aimed at mitigating emissions , generating energy and exploiting the possibilities of recycling . <p> Sadly , there 's precious little sign of these in Ireland . <p> Our policy , every fucking time , is to stick with the known and avoid anything new or risky , even if it might actually deliver the results more efficiently and effectively . Look at our offshore wind policy . Where are the floating wind turbines ? <h> Advertisement <p> Where are the many emerging small and vertical turbine technologies that can be incorporated into the design of housing schemes , shopping centres and office complexes ? <p> Well , the next Government must follow through without fear or favour . <p> Otherwise we 're stuck with the hard rain ... and worse . <p> Read the full Whole Hog End of Year Special in the Hot Press Annual 2025 -- out now :

@@119267917 <h> An Irishwoman sailing around the world : ' This paradise has just seven residents and two dogs ' <h> Dubliner Kate Ashe-Leonard left Ireland in 2017 to live with her partner in London . In 2018 , they began their adventure to sail around the world <p> In 2018 , Kate Ashe-Leonard and her partner Jim began their adventure to sail around the world <p> Kate Ashe-Leonard <p> Wed Dec 25 2024 - 06:00 <p> The tiny coral atoll of Maupiha'a lies 120 nautical miles west of Bora Bora 's five-star over-water bungalows . This paradise rises only a few feet above sea level and , with just seven residents and two dogs , it 's no tourist hotspot . <p> Helming our sailboat , we make a careful approach with the help of our chart plotter and satellite imagery . Compared to our own technology-heavy circumnavigation , I 'm in awe of the early Polynesian settlers . More than two thousand years ago , in wooden outrigger canoes , they navigated this vast ocean using the stars as their guide . <p> Polynesia , subregion of Oceania , is made up of more than 1,000 islands scattered over the central and southern Pacific Ocean <p> Access to the atoll 's interior is via a narrow passage where the ocean floods in and ebbs out on the tide and capricious currents swirl menacingly . Furling away our sails , we engage our engines . As we accelerate , steep underwater coral walls either side of us are illuminated by scattered beams of sunlight . <p> Placing six parrot fish neatly on our back step , Harry and Norma introduce themselves , inviting us to their place " tout moment " before vanishing . <p> Since arriving in this country 14 months ago , the interchange between languages is a constant reminder that French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France . Recently , the pro-independence party came into power and it 's not difficult to understand some of the reasons why . That 193 atomic bombs were detonated by the French , contaminating atolls like this one until 1996 , is the most horrifying one to me . <p> Maupiha ? a is an atoll in the Leeward group of the Society Islands in the South Pacific . <p> Sending ripples across the glassy lagoon , we startle a green turtle and two burrowing stingrays . Through knee-deep water , over coral-pink sand , we wade , dragging our paddle-boards up the beach . <p> Crafted from woven palm fronds , a little house sits pleasantly under shady overhanging trees . Rows of vegetables , planted in sandy soil , span an impressive variety and nearby , a tiny generator , rainwater catchment system and solar panels complete the technological array . <p> Kate Ashe-Leonard left Ireland in 2017 <p> I open my bag placing a contribution on the table -- flour , mayonnaise , cooking oil , fishing hooks and two spare knives . A black terrier barks playfully until Norma appears , shushing the mutt who 's tied to a tree . Punishment , apparently , for gobbling the remaining chickens . <p> Barefoot , we explore the airless palm forest that runs parallel to the ocean . Machetes and other tools for de-husking coconuts litter the path . A lapis lazuli-coloured coconut crab emerges from a pile of fallen fronds snapping its claws at me . Further along coconut flesh dries in the sun being transformed into what 's known as Copra . <p> On our return , four green coconuts have been set on a table , a drinking hole punched out of each . <p> We begin to chat . Their home atoll , Maupiti , is just 95 nautical miles away . They 're here to harvest Copra . With a weighty quota to meet before the Copra ship will come for them , and only seven people to process it , two years has passed since they 've been home . <p> But they do seem content . They say , this place gives them everything they need . <p> " Socialising with sailors is important though . " Norma explains . <p> Through our patchy French and with the aid of paper and pencils , we exchange stories of our adventures . Us transients , I realise , are their link to the outside world . <p> One evening , under a waxing gibbous moon , Harry leads us through the coconut palms . He 's been fattening up coconut crabs in traps . Keeping all fingers intact , masterfully he handles them into netted bags . <p> This is how , in 1991 , the residents survived cyclone Wasa-Arthur 's eight-metre waves that submerged all but the tallest treetops . <p> The tiny coral atoll of Mauipha'a lies 120 nautical miles west of Bora Bora <p> The tiny coral atoll of Mauipha'a lies 120 nautical miles west of Bora Bora <p> Life here is precarious : climate change brings more frequent cyclones , while storms from thousands of miles away create surges capable of engulfing an atoll like this one . Without access to weather forecasting , like their Polynesians ancestors , they look to nature 's signals ; the behaviour of wildlife , the angle and movement of trees , cloud formations and the sea state . <p> On the 12th night , an east wind blows -- the time for our onward journey to Samoa has arrived . Coconuts and papayas are packed into our dinghy , a gift from Maupiha'a we 're told . A guestbook containing sailors ' messages of gratitude dating back years is passed to us to sign . <p> The roar of the Pacific beckons us to walk the outer reef one last time . I watch the night sky mirrored in rock pools and beyond the whitewash of a thousand breaking waves . At first light we 'll weigh anchor , all the richer for the time spent with these resilient and generous hosts in this wild place . <p> Kate Ashe-Leonard left Ireland in 2017 to live with her partner Jim in London . In 2018 , they began their adventure to sail around the world . They initially intended to take a three-year sabbatical from work , but after five years it has become a new way of life . They have lived off rental income from their home in London and working remotely . @@119280003 <h> Turning the tide of habitat restoration in south Mayo <p> Published:Wed 25 Dec 2024 , 9:00 AM <p> The D ? lra project , a flagship initiative for invasive species control and habitat restoration , has restored over 1,000 hectares of blanket bog in and around Special Areas of Conservation across Galway and Mayo in 2024 . <p> Managed by FORUM Connemara CLG , in partnership with the Leenane Development Association , the D ? lra Project is part of the Natura Communities initiative funded by the National Parks and Wildlife Service ( NPWS ) via LIFE IP Wild Atlantic Nature . <p> The D ? lra Project employs locals and engages local communities in transformative habitat restoration and control of invasive rhododendron , marking a major step in biodiversity conservation in Ireland . <p> " This essential funding from NPWS enabled us to hire and train a dedicated team of 20 local operatives , who carried out extensive work successfully treating rhododendron across Connemara and parts of southwest Mayo , " said Sin ? ad Grimes , D ? lra Project Manager . <p> Highlighting the importance of the funding , Grimes added : " Without this support , these critical works simply would not have been possible . <p> " This funding not only facilitated on-the-ground action but also enabled local communities to do the work by providing training , employment and skills development opportunities in conservation . <p> " Through this project , we 've reclaimed over 1,000 hectares of ecologically sensitive lands from invasive rhododendron ; and trained locals in the skills needed to carry out maintenance , this is a real win for local communities . " <p> The D ? lra team recently completed the first phase of the project 's rhododendron control efforts in southwest Mayo . <p> Over a three-week period between October 29 and November 22 , a dedicated team of 10 professionals worked in difficult conditions to manage the invasive Rhododendron ponticum , treating a total of approximately 360 hectares ( ha ) within the Mweelrea/Sheeffry/Erriff Complex Special Area of Conservation ( SAC ) . <p> Further work is planned in 2025 to finalise these works in the area . <p> A second team was simultaneously working in South Connemara to clear lands in the Connemara Bog Complex SAC . <p> The team have previously cleared both commonage and private lands at various locations around the Twelve Bens/Garraun Complex and Mweelrea/Sheeffry/Erriff Complex SACs and hope to expand into the Maumturk Mountains and Lough Corrib SAC areas in the coming years . <p> The team employ the stem herbicide application method for controlling rhododendron as recommended by the National Parks and Wildlife Service ( NPWS ) . <p> However , the team are unique in that they are the only group in Ireland making biochar with the cut rhododendron brash . <p> Biochar is a stable , carbon-rich material produced by heating organic matter , such as wood or plant waste , in a low-oxygen environment through a process called pyrolysis . <p> This innovative approach ensures that greenhouse gases , which would otherwise be released as the brash decomposes , are instead captured and locked into the biochar . <p> Remarkably , up to 88% of the carbon from the rhododendron is effectively removed from the carbon cycle . <p> By converting the biomass into biochar , the carbon is sequestered in a solid form that resists decomposition for hundreds of years . <p> This helps mitigate climate change by reducing the amount of carbon dioxide and methane released into the atmosphere . <p> Biochar is a versatile material with a wide range of uses . It can improve soil fertility and structure by enhancing water retention , nutrient availability , and microbial activity . <p> Additionally , biochar is used in water filtration , livestock feed supplements , and even as a component in construction materials . <p> This makes the team 's work not only environmentally significant but also a valuable contribution to sustainable resource management . <p> Project collaborator and head of Leenane Development Association , Martin Gavin , a farmer from Leenane , expressed gratitude for the collective effort : " This work represents a critical step in restoring our ecosystems . <p> " The participation of landowners and the collaboration between the community , NPWS , Wild Atlantic Nature and the D ? lra team have been instrumental in achieving this success . We are proud of the progress and look forward to continuing these efforts in 2025 . " <p> The D ? lra Project remains committed to combating invasive species and protecting the region 's biodiversity . <p> " While significant progress has been made , follow-up work and community engagement will be essential to ensure the continued success of these efforts . <p> The D ? lra project continues to make significant strides in tackling invasive species and demonstrating the value of collaborative efforts in ecological restoration to protect Ireland 's unique natural landscapes . <p> For more details on the project or to learn how you can get involved , visit the D ? lra Project Website on https : **29;917;TOOLONG or email dulra@forumconnemara.ie . <p> Published:Wed 25 Dec 2024 , 9:00 AM <p> Our Connaught Telegraph compact edition is out every Tuesday with the latest news , sport and entertainment in Castlebar and Mayo . 
@@119296383 <h> 2024 shaping up to be one of Ireland 's warmest years on record despite unusually cool summer <p> A person on a slipway in Clontarf , Dublin , as Storm Darragh approached . Damage to Holyhead by the storm has caused logistical headaches on both sides of the Irish Sea . Photo : AP <p> Caroline O'Doherty <p> Yesterday at 03:30 <p> With just days to go , 2024 is shaping up to be one of Ireland 's top 10 warmest years on record . <p> It is unlikely to be remembered for high temperatures , however , as more notable events included an unusually cool summer , a code red storm , a flash flood and even a mini-drought . <p> The top 10 placing , which Met ? ireann expects to declare if there are no surprises before the end of the month , comes despite a summer dominated by Arctic air masses that pulled temperatures down . <p> " We 're in a period now when even when it seems cool , overall temperatures are above the long-term average , " Paul Moore , climatologist with Met ? ireann , said . <p> A person on a slipway in Clontarf , Dublin , as Storm Darragh approached . Damage to Holyhead by the storm has caused logistical headaches on both sides of the Irish Sea . Photo : AP <p> 7-Day Weather Forecast : 23rd December - 29th December 2024 <p> His point is illustrated by the one month that will enter the record books -- May , which was the country 's ? warmest May since recording began . Many would be surprised to hear that , because it was a cloudy and dull month with no real scorchers . <p> " It was warm because the night-time temperatures were very high , " Mr Moore said . <p> " We did n't have lots of warm , sunny days -- it was warm , cloudy days and then warm nights , with the cloud acting as insulation . " <p> He said that sea surface temperatures in the Atlantic , which experienced an unprecedented extreme marine heatwave last year , were still well above average . <p> " So when we get the air masses coming from there , as we often do , we tend to get above-average temperatures , " he said . <p> The build-up of heat caused thunderstorms and intense bursts of rain in the second and third weeks of the month -- one of several bouts of thunder that occurred during the year . <p> It was not warm air from the ? Atlantic that shaped the next few months , however , but cold air from the north . <p> While much of Europe had its warmest summer on record in a year that was the world 's hottest overall , this country was an outlier . The heat from mainland Europe did n't reach Ireland , which was mostly stuck on the northerly side of the jet stream and was chilled by Arctic blasts . " High pressure tended to build to our west with low pressure over Scandinavia and that brought down cold air , " Mr Moore said . <p> " If high pressure was to the east then hot air might come up from the south , but we did n't tap into any of those hot continental air masses during the summer . " <p> There were some notably warm days this year -- particularly those that popped up during winter months . <p> Belmullet hit a balmy 15.4C on ? January 28 -- the highest ever recorded for a January day in that location and a curveball in a month when temperatures were otherwise below average overall . <p> Moore Park in Cork recorded 14.7C in February and seven of Met ? ireann 's 25 main weather stations had their warmest February on record . Five had their warmest in 25 years and nine had their highest-ever minimum night-time temperature , which never fell below -- 2.2C . <p> A narrower-than-normal gap between day and night temperatures was also a feature in March and April . <p> More recently , temperatures reached 19.1C in Athenry on October 16 and a remarkable 19.2C in Dublin 's Phoenix Park on November 6 . <p> This year has also been notable for storms , beginning with Storm Isha , which struck on January 21 and was followed just three days later by Storm Jocelyn . Western and north-western counties were worst hit during this period and fallen power lines left tens of thousands without electricity , some for several days . <p> Storm Kathleen struck in early April and Lilian arrived in August followed by Ashley in October , Bert in November and the biggest of them all , Darragh . <p> Storm Darragh , which blasted through most of the country during the first week of this month had multiple counties under red wind warnings and deservedly so . <p> Many trees came down across the country and at one point almost 400,000 customers were without power . <p> Thousands still had no electricity days later and the impact on neighbouring Britain is continuing to be felt here in the disruption caused by damage to Holyhead port . <p> Two other storms , Henk in January and Conall in November , were also on Ireland 's radar , but they skirted around the country , causing little more than a stiff breeze . <p> Storm damage might have been worse only for the fact that in most cases the accompanying rain was less extreme than experienced in previous years . That was n't the case in Donegal , however , where heavy rain during Storm Bert caused flooding in several parts , most dramatically in Killybegs . <p> The River Feale rose so rapidly that it burst its banks and inundated homes and businesses before anyone had a chance to sound a warning or move to protect their property and belongings . <p> Yet even in Donegal , overall rainfall was below average , as it was in all but four of Met ? ireann 's main stations over the year . <p> Many stations had official " dry spells " , which means 15 or more consecutive days with less than a millimetre of rain each . <p> One area , Moore Park in Co Cork , was officially declared to be in drought in January with 16 days when every day had no rain or less than 0.2mm of rain . <p> February , March and April were wetter than average and parts of Donegal and Wexford received almost twice their normal monthly rainfall . <p> June and July were cool and dry in most places , but August saw the country split , with the west and north getting a good deal of rain while the east and south received little . <p> The pattern flipped in September with the north and west the driest , and the south and east wettest . <p> It was mostly cool all over and there was an usually early autumn frost , but since then , temperatures have been mainly mild . <p> Last year was Ireland 's hottest and wettest on record , with a mean temperature of 11.2C . Mr Moore said that would not be repeated this year , but he said temperatures were still generally moving in the same direction -- upwards -- as the evidence of climate change becomes ever more pronounced . <p> The outlook for 2025 is uncertain , although it is expected that overall global temperatures may be marginally lower than this year , which was under the influence of El Ni ? o for the first half . <p> El Ni ? o is a natural climatic variation caused by the movement of warm air from the Pacific and it helped supercharge the already climbing temperatures of the last two years . <p> Its opposite , La Ni ? a , generally has a cooling effect , but scientists have said that if a La Ni ? a develops in 2025 , they are not confident it will substantially counteract the human-caused warming of the world . <p> " Even if a La Ni ? a event does emerge , its short-term cooling impact will be insufficient to counterbalance the warming effect of record heat-trapping greenhouse gases in the atmosphere , " Celeste Saulo , of the World Meteorological Organisation , said . " Even in the absence of El Ni ? o or La Ni ? a , conditions since May , we have witnessed an extraordinary series of extreme weather events which have unfortunately become the new norm in our changing climate . "

It 's a consistent problem : Up to one-third of food that comes into a home goes into the bin and this only gets worse at Christmas time . <p> " It 's the most wasteful time of the year , " says Waterford-based chef and author Conor Spacey . <p> " There 's a lot of food waste anyway but at Christmas it 's accelerated . While Christmas is a celebration based around family , friends , and food , now it 's also marketed to us as a time of overconsumption -- of food in particular -- that we really do n't need . " <p> At this time of the year , there 's a definite air of wish fulfilment in all the glossy supermarket promotional pamphlets . Do we need chicken bao and brie tartlets , prawn garlands , complicated cauliflower cheese , stuffings suffused with musty dried herbs , and enough cakes , puddings , and all-butter mince pies to cause any Stephen 's Day swimmer to sink like very well-fed stones ? <p> Perhaps not , but piled high and sold at as a three-for-two special offer , it 's hard to resist . <p> " We buy so much without actually really planning , " says Spacey . " People say , ' yes , I need lots of food ! ' and it 's the big Christmas lunch which puts the fear of god into a lot of people . You do n't need to buy that much . Do you really have to get food in case John and Mary call round , or Paddy next door arrives ? <p> Very few homes have space to store food excess properly and then there 's a risk of things going off . " <p> For Spacey , festive feasting revolves around the main event : " It 's about planning . We do n't want to be cooking from scratch -- I 'm not going to cook a different meal every day over the holidays . It 's about being smart about it . But , aside from any environmental impacts , throwing away food also has financial repercussions . <p> While we may be aware that wasted food contributes to increased greenhouse gas -- between eight to 10% of annual global greenhouse gas emissions , according to the 2024 UN food waste index report -- and that reducing food waste has a role to play in climate change and addressing global food insecurity , it also has a significant impact on our pocket . <p> " It 's an expensive time of the year , " says Spacey . " Say an average week 's shop of ? 150 to ? 200 for a family will double over Christmas week . But how much of that will be thrown away ? It 's like if I handed you a ? 50 note and said , ' throw that in the bin ' . It does n't matter your situation is you definitely do n't want to be throwing money away . Put it into a pie dish with cooked sliced potatoes on top and bake ; <p> If you have extra roast potatoes , make them into hash . Mix some melted chocolate with the crumbled pudding and roll into bite-sized truffles.
