@@119397287 <h> COMMENT : The EU 's Green Deal is a " policy disaster " <p> The EU 's Green Deal is based on a renewable only solution to emissions reduction and relies on technology that does n't exist , argues energy analyst Tom O'Donnell , an advisor to several governments in Europe . The whole policy needs to be rethought and nuclear power has to be part of the answer . / bne IntelliNews <p> By bne IntelliNewsDecember 29 , 2024 <p> Energy analyst Dr Tom O'Donnell has issued a stark critique of the European Union 's Green Deal , describing it as a " policy disaster " that requires radical reform to prevent further industrial decline and to bolster energy security . <p> " Several of the stated key technical requirements for the model to succeed have failed , " O'Donnell stated , pointing to the lack of universally applicable , long-term , grid-scale storage technology as a critical flaw . <p> He traced the origins of the EU 's Green Deal to the German Energiewende , itself influenced by American physicist Amory Lovins ' " Soft Energy Paths " concept from the 1970s . <p> " In 2019 , Dr. Lovins , an American physicist and futurist , was decorated by the German government , recognized as the father , in effect , of the plan that has become the German national energy transition policy . He is also credited with coining the phrase " energy transition " , " Donnell said . <p> The initial reason for advocating this soft-energy-paths transition had very little to do with climate change . Climate change was a minor issue at the time . Rather , it had to do with how , in order to use hard energy paths , you need big industrial facilities run by big corporations . So , it was said that to undermine these corporations ' power , we have to use only renewables , says Donnell . <p> At that time in Germany , an anti-big business movement had grown up against the arbitrariness of large project decisions by government and corporations , without any local consultations with citizens that was a backlash against the rapid post-war re-industrialization . <p> In addition , neo-Malthusian ideas , first popularized by the Club of Rome , had popularized predictions of the extinction of each mineral resource , including oil and gas , as well as another looming overpopulation crisis . <p> " These deep-seated concerns were the bases of what , in Germany in particular , coalesced into a new movement for replacing so-called " hard energy paths , " fossil fuels and nuclear power , as a path to preserving the environment and killing the economic and social dominance of large corporations , " says Donnell . " Climate change , as an issue , as a driver of this all-renewables program , came along later . " <p> O'Donnell argued that , despite decades of research and development , essential technologies such as advanced grid-scale storage and smart grids have not materialised at the necessary scale . <p> Two core ideas of the soft energy paths were smart " mini-grids " and developing effective power storage . Mini-grids are democratic energy , set up to serve a community and run by the community . From the start it was clear the drawback with renewables is the intermittent nature of its energy -- there is only power when the sun shines and the wind blows . Smart meters attached to the mini-grid would tell housewives when they can run the washing machine or a factory 's machinery . Essentially , communities would sync activity to the weather . <p> Even then it was clear from the start that in addition is the need for grid storage of power to deal with demand that will inevitably run above renewable energy supply in peak periods of the day and to deal with what the Germans call " Dunkelflaute , " the days when the sun does n't shine and winds lull . Battery technology has come a long way in the last forty years , but today it can cope with an hour of poor weather conditions but it is still nowhere near being able to cope with Dunkelflaute at any kind of scale . <p> Other than batteries the best energy storage technology is pumped storage hydropower that currently accounts for 93% of all grid-scale storage capacity . But pumped storage is only suitable for countries with large mountainous lakes . However , pumped storage is not an option for all the countries between Paris and Moscow on the Great Northern Plain , which is as flat as a pancake . <p> For all these reasons , Europe remains hooked on Russian gas as the best alternative energy source and the least harmful for the climate . Despite its best efforts to wean itself off Russian gas in the last two years , Russian gas increased its share in the EU energy mix over 2024 from 14% at the start of the year to 21.2% in December . <p> The 8th Monitoring Report of the Energiewende report that tracks Germany 's progress in the national energy transition program presented to former Chancellor Angela Merkel concluded that Germany can not produce sufficient renewables on its own territory to satisfy its own demand for power . It will always have to import power , putting increased strain on other EU members that are also struggling to reduce fossil fuel use . <p> In lieu of sufficient renewable generating capacity last year Robert Habeck , a leader of the Green Party , got emergency parliament funding to install 25GW of new natural gas generation ( he actually wanted 36-39GW ) , roughly equal to 25 big coal plants or 25 big nuclear plants and a de facto abandonment of the " renewables only " policy that has driven German energy transition policy until now . <p> In desperation , the Merkel government launched a " hydrogen strategy " as an alternative to gas , but as bne IntelliNews reported hydrogen wo n't work due to numerous technical problems . To name only one , it ca n't be transported as to liquify it , hydrogen needs to be cooled to just 20C over absolute zero , needing an extraordinarily amount of energy to make it that cold . Only helium has a lower liquification point . And as hydrogen atoms are so small , they simply leak through the walls of conventional pipelines , posing a major explosion threat . <p> The only realistic scalable alternative to natural gas or renewables is nuclear power following France 's Messmer model , argues O'Donnell . <p> Barking up the wrong tree <p> Since these early days , the mini-grid idea has been abandoned and replaced with the idea of a as large a grid as possible to smooth out the local variants in supply and so smooth supply . Germany 's decision to switch off its six nuclear power plants and becoming a net importer was made possible as EU rules forced its neighbours to export Germany the missing power . Now this winter , countries like Sweden , Norway and the Baltic states have begun to complain heavily after the cost of power in their countries has soared . <p> " The idea was that you could get rid of all of what Lovins called ' hard energy paths , ' that is fossil fuels and nuclear , and replace this with so-called ' soft energy paths , ' meaning renewables , " Donnell . <p> O'Donnell warned that the EU 's steadfast commitment to an all-renewables strategy , without addressing these technological gaps , is leading to deindustrialisation and undermining energy security . <p> He cited Germany 's recent closure of its last three nuclear power plants during a wartime energy crisis as an example of policy decisions that exacerbate the problem . <p> " The stance that the new Commission is taking , while focusing on energy and industrial policy , is simply doubling down on old policies , wrong policies which are dangerous , " O'Donnell asserted . <p> He criticised the appointment of Teresa Ribera , a proponent of all-renewable energy systems , as the European Commission 's Executive Vice-President in charge of both the Green Deal and industrialisation . <p> " The fact that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen fought hard to appoint Ribera and then put her in charge ... shows that Von der Leyen ... has no interest in reform of the renewables model despite its suffering technological failures on several key aspects , " O'Donnell remarked . " The problem is , Ms. Ribera is a true believer in all-renewable energy systems , I would say a career-long renewable fundamentalist " <p> " She 's said to be so good at negotiating that she managed to get the Spanish nuclear industry and civil society to agree on a timetable to close all the Spanish nuclear power plants , and she 's very proud of this , " O'Donnell added . <p> This misguided policy is condemning Germany and the rest of Europe to deindustrialisation , a process that already started long before the war in Ukraine catalysed it with the 2022 energy crisis . The point was rammed home in great detail by the report by former Italian Prime Minister and ex-European Central Bank boss Mario Draghi that warned Europe has lost its competitive edge and needs to spend ? 800bn a year to just stand still , or about 4% of Europe 's collective GDP . Finding this amount of money is a daunting prospect for budgets that have already been depleted first by the 2020 pandemic and now by the ? 100bn a year sent to Kyiv . And all this comes at a time as all of Europe sinks into recession . <p> " Von der Leyen 's administration has no new ideas on this , and is instead simply changing names of things from " green " to " clean " and doubling down on the technologically failed Green Deal Model , based on the German Energiewende Model , " says O'Donnell . " EU strategy , as Ribera and Von der Leyen repeatedly remind us , is to use green tech development to regain EU competitiveness . But , that battle for Green tech supremacy has already been lost . You know the story vis- ? -vis both the USA and especially China ... And so , there was , and still is , a wrong theory , a flawed model , and it is now contributing to the deindustrialization of Europe , to its competitive failures . " <p> The failure to recognise the flaws in the EU 's green transition policies is leading to the deindustrialization of Europe . That in turn presents an acute economic and national security threat for Europe . The German industrial decline will pull everybody else down , especially their Central and Eastern Europe ( CEE ) and Baltic neighbours simply because it is so big and so important as a market to all its neighbours , O'Donnell argues . <p> As a solution , O'Donnell advocated for a diversified energy mix that includes nuclear power , citing France 's historical success in decarbonising its electricity generation through nuclear energy without the need for new grids or long-term storage technologies . <p> " The French Messmer plan , which rapidly built nuclear plants , succeeded in decarbonising French electrical generation without any need for new grids or long-term grid-scale storage tech , " he noted . <p> O'Donnell 's critique calls for a reassessment of the EU 's current energy policies to address technological shortcomings and to consider a more pragmatic approach that ensures both energy security and industrial competitiveness . <h> Opinion <h> Having a reliable electricity supply is something many of us take for granted -- including for sending and reading emails like this one . But hundreds of millions of people around the world today do n't have access to electricity . <h> In what looks like a very good deal for Blackrock , the private equity house has bought the diamond certification company IGI for $569mn and will likely monetised approximately $324mn from the IPO while still owning around 84% of a $2.1bn business . <h> Reports <h> Cookies on the bne IntelliNews website <p> This site uses cookies - small text files that are placed on your machine to help the site provide a better user experience . @@119397498 <h> There 's reasons to be hopeful about tackling climate change in 2025 -- honestly <p> Can the world avoid a disastrous three degree temperature rise ? And will Labour 's climate plans work in the UK ? Climate expert Bob Ward lays out what 2025 holds <p> by : Bob Ward <p> 29 Dec 2024 <p> Labour has laid out ambitious climate plans . But what do they hold for 2025 ? Image : Dan Dennison/DESNZ/Flickr <p> Share <p> The world 's battle against climate change suffered major setbacks in 2024 but there are glimmers of hope ahead . <p> The global temperature over the past year was the warmest on record and , significantly , exceeded the 1.5 Celsius degree rise in temperature compared with pre-industrial level that international efforts have been trying to avoid . <p> This record temperature was boosted by the natural warming caused by the El Ni ? o in the first half of the year , and 2025 is expected to be slightly cooler . But the global temperature is expected to be consistently more than 1.5 Celsius degrees warmer within the next couple of decades . <p> Annual global emissions of carbon dioxide , the main driver of climate change , also reached record levels in 2024 , although the rate of increase appears to have slowed in recent years , suggesting that we may be close to the peak . <p> However , the rise in global temperature and other impacts of climate change will continue to increase until annual emissions effectively reach zero . Many countries have set a target of reaching ' net zero ' emissions by 2050 . <p> The mounting impacts of climate change are now evident all around the globe . The surface waters of the North Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico were extremely warm in late 2024 , contributing to a very destructive hurricane season . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> Many people were killed and injured , and billions of dollars of damage were caused , by hurricanes that rapidly intensified over the warm waters and smashed into the coast of the United States . <p> Even Donald Trump commented on the scale of the destruction in Florida from Hurricane Helene in September , but he continued to deny the reality of climate change during his successful campaign for president . <p> Trump is widely expected to withdraw the United States , the world 's second largest emitter of greenhouse gases after China , from the landmark Paris Agreement which countries reached in 2015 to try to avoid the worst impacts of climate change . <p> This means the United States is unlikely to submit a more ambitious pledge for action ahead of the COP30 United Nations climate change summit in Bel ? m , Brazil , in November 2025 . <p> The Paris Agreement commits all countries to offer plans for stronger action , or " nationally-determined contributions " , in 2025 . Current plans are collectively too weak and would mean warming of about three degrees Celsius by the end of the century . <p> That would result in a global temperature that was last experienced on Earth about three million years during the Pliocene Epoch , when global sea level was five to 25 metres higher than today . <p> Advertisement <p> However , countries struggled at the COP29 United Nations climate change summit in Baku , Azerbaijan , in November 2024 to agree an increase in financial support to help developing countries to improve their plans for action . <p> Many countries will be looking towards the European Union and China for international leadership on climate change if the Trump administration does step back and turn inwards . <p> China is by far the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases , but also has more renewable energy and electric vehicles than any other country . <p> The new Labour government in the United Kingdom has been attempting to demonstrate international leadership on climate action by already announcing in Baku a plan to cut its annual emissions of greenhouse gases by 81% by 2035 compared with 1990 . <p> In order to help achieve this goal , the government has set a very ambitious target to stop any emissions from the power sector by 2030 , primarily through a massive increase in renewable energy . <p> However it faces many challenges , including the difficulties of building transmission lines from new wind and solar farms to connect to the electricity grid . <p> Advertisement <p> In addition , the government will seek the accelerate the roll-out of other zero-emissions technologies , such as electric vehicles and heat pumps . <p> The government will also face calls to cut the price of electricity , which is higher in the UK than in most other countries . <p> The UK 's current system means that electricity prices are usually set by natural gas , which is generally more expensive than renewables . <p> With household energy prices set to rise again in January 2025 , increasing the rate of inflation , the UK 's future prosperity and energy security will be boosted by accelerating the transition away from expensive imports of fossil fuels and towards cheap and clean domestic energy . <p> And there is a hope that other countries will follow the UK 's example in 2025 , helping the world to turn the corner in its desperate battle against climate change , 10 years after the Paris Agreement set the target of stopping greenhouse gas emissions . <p> Bob Ward is policy and communications director at the Grantham Research Institute on climate change and the environment at the London School of Economics and Political Science .

@@119429584 <p> Greenland is crumbling before our eyes . This frozen giant is melting at an alarming rate , with significant implications for global sea levels . <p> New research reveals a stark reality : between 2010 and 2023 , Greenland lost a staggering 563 cubic miles ( 2,347 cubic kilometers ) of ice . That 's enough water to fill Lake Victoria , Africa 's largest lake . <p> The video visualization highlights the areas of greatest ice loss through the darkest red color . <p> This research is a collaborative effort between NASA and the European Space Agency ( ESA ) . The video was put together using data from two powerful satellites -- ESA 's CryoSat-2 and NASA 's ICESat-2 -- that continuously monitor Greenland 's changing landscape . <p> CryoSat-2 uses radar , while ICESat-2 employs laser technology to measure the height of the ice sheet . <h> Melting glacier edges <p> The nearly 40-second video showcases that the edges of the ice sheet are bearing the brunt of this melting crisis . Over the years , the edges of the ice sheet experienced a 21-foot ( 6.4-meter ) loss in thickness on average . <p> The study aimed to go beyond simply measuring ice loss . Recognizing the strengths and weaknesses of both satellite measurement techniques ( radar and laser ) , researchers sought to validate their compatibility by ensuring consistent results . <p> This validation step was crucial for a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of ice loss in Greenland . <p> The study demonstrated high levels of agreement between the two satellite measurements . This strong concordance allowed for the combination of their data , revealing an average ice sheet thinning of 3.9 feet ( 1.2 meters ) over the 13-year study period . <p> " It is great to see that the data from ' sister missions ' are providing a consistent picture of the changes going on in Greenland , " said Thorsten Markus , project scientist for the ICESat-2 mission at NASA , in the press statement . <p> Understanding the magnitude of this crisis is crucial . This will help prepare for and adapt to the impacts of climate change . Therefore , access to accurate , up-to-date ice sheet change data is highly important . <p> " As ice sheet mass loss is a key contributor to global sea level rise , this is incredibly useful for the scientific community and policymakers , " said Nitin Ravinder , the lead author from the UK Centre for Polar Observation and Modelling ( CPOM ) , in the press release . <h> The Blueprint Daily <h> ABOUT THE EDITOR <p> Mrigakshi Dixit Mrigakshi is a science journalist who enjoys writing about space exploration , biology , and technological innovations . When we might speak of peace in a diverse world , where the safety and dignity of every human being is valued . This is now our best hope and preparation for responsible and sustainable lives together on what is our vulnerable shared planet . <p> When I addressed the UN Summit on the Future of the United Nations in New York in September , I spoke of authenticity , of how our urgent interacting crises require us to recover a lost authenticity between words and actions , to draw on what were our better , promising moments of achieving trust , such as in 2015 when we agreed collectively the United Nations 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals , a shared blueprint for peace and human development in recognising and responding to the consequences of climate change and the promise of sustainable living . <p> We are challenged however by the fact that our delivery on these Goals has been so much less than what was committed . Today , just 17 percent of the Sustainable Development Goals are currently on track . Half of the 17 goals are showing " minimal or moderate progress " , while over a third are either " stalled or regressing " . <p> The failure to achieve peace , to eliminate acute global poverty , hunger , and the consequences of climate change and biodiversity loss have been accompanied by a return to an arms race , to a world that has rewarded investors in instruments of death rather than promoting sustainability . <p> Now is the time for all of us , for all peoples to speak and urge countries of the world who wish to see a world of peace , a sustainable and more equal world built on the Sustainable Development Goals , to come together , speak out and force the measures that will make these vital goals a global achievement . <p> May I take this opportunity to thank all those who sent messages of good wishes for the health of Sabina and I over the last year -- your warmth and encouragement was deeply appreciated by us both . <p> - Advertisement - <p> 2024 marked ten years since I made a return State Visit to the United Kingdom in 2014 , the first such visit by a President of Ireland to the UK , and following three years after the State Visit made by the late Queen Elizabeth II to Ireland in 2011 . <p> I was pleased to mark that anniversary with a visit to Manchester last April , where I received an Honorary Doctorate from the University of Manchester -- a university where I undertook post-graduate studies from 1968 to 1971 -- and to have the chance to again meet with some of the Irish community both in that city and from Britain more broadly . <p> My warmest wishes for a peaceful and happy New Year to all of the Irish community in Britain <p> As I enter this 14th and final year as President of Ireland , it remains the greatest honour and privilege to serve the Irish people . I look forward immensely to continuing to do so over the coming year . <p> During my terms in Office , both Sabina and I have experienced and valued the warmth and friendship of people both at home and abroad , including in each of our visits to Britain . We have witnessed the resilience , compassion , creativity , empathy and kindness of Irish people across the globe in so many different ways . @@119456020 <h> The Increasing Demand for Pest Control in Dublin <p> In recent years , Dublin has witnessed an unsettling rise in pest activity , with many residents and businesses struggling with unwanted infestations . From the persistent and annoying insects to the destructive and disease-ridden rodents , pests are no longer just an occasional nuisance . They have become a significant concern , threatening not only public health but also the city 's infrastructure and economy . <p> As the city 's population swells and urban development accelerates , the very conditions that make it an attractive place to live and work are also proving to be a magnet for these unwelcome intruders . This increase in pest problems demands urgent attention and effective solutions to safeguard the city 's future . <p> The Impact of Increased Pest Activity in Dublin <p> According to Ultimate Pest Control Dublin , the negative and costly impact of increased pest infestations is being felt across homes , businesses , and public spaces in Dublin . <p> Impact on Public Health <p> One of the most significant concerns associated with pest infestations in the city is the threat they pose to public health . Pests such as rats and mice are known to carry various diseases that can easily spread through contaminated food , surfaces , or direct contact . <p> Insects , too , play a role in spreading harmful bacteria . Flies , for instance , are notorious for transporting pathogens from waste and filth to food , potentially causing foodborne illnesses . <p> Economic Consequences <p> The economic toll of rising pest populations is another crucial aspect of this problem . Infestations can lead to significant financial losses for both homeowners and businesses . For homeowners , pests can cause damage to electrical wiring , insulation , and even the structural components of buildings , leading to costly repairs . They can also cause damage to personal property and valuables . <p> In commercial properties , such as retail stores , warehouses , or restaurants , pests can destroy goods and inventory , particularly in the food sector , where contamination risks are high . <p> Pest infestations in hospitality businesses , such as hotels and restaurants , can be particularly detrimental to their reputation leading to significant loss of sales . In addition , it can lead to health code violations and hefty fines . <p> Impact on Quality of Life <p> For residents , the psychological and emotional toll of dealing with pests is significant . The presence of rats , mice , or insects in the home can lead to increased stress , anxiety , and a diminished quality of life . People may feel embarrassed or unsafe in their own homes , which can affect their overall wellbeing . <p> Environmental Impact <p> The rising need for pest control in Dublin has led to an increased use of chemical pesticides , which , while effective , have led to unintended consequences for the environment including , contamination of soil and water and harm to beneficial insects like bees . <p> Additionally , invasive pests pose the risk of disrupting local ecosystems by outcompeting native species for resources , threatening biodiversity . <p> Common Pests in Dublin <p> Dublin faces a range of pest problems that impact homes , businesses , and public spaces . Seagulls , in particular , are a growing nuisance , as their numbers increase in cities . This expansion often leads to the destruction of natural habitats , forcing pests into urban environments . With more people living in close quarters , it becomes easier for pests to spread from one property to another , increasing the risk of infestations . <p> Poor Waste Management <p> Improper waste disposal and poor hygiene practices are also contributing to the pest problem in Dublin according to Moovmor Recycling . During lockdowns , many businesses closed their doors , leaving behind vacant spaces that became breeding grounds for pests . According to reports , there has been a 40% increase in rat control treatments since the onset of the pandemic , as rodents took advantage of deserted urban areas . <p> Climate Change <p> The impact of climate change is another factor contributing to the rise in pests . Warmer winters and more humid summers provide a more favourable environment for pests to survive and reproduce . Insects like cockroaches and ants thrive in these conditions , while rodents are more likely to seek shelter in urban areas during milder winters . These changes in weather patterns have extended the breeding seasons for many pests , allowing them to multiply at a faster rate . <p> Challenges in Addressing the Pest Infestation Problem in Dublin <p> Lack of Awareness <p> Many residents and businesses in Dublin may not immediately recognise the early signs of pest infestations , which can lead to more severe problems down the line . For instance , a single rat or cockroach sighting might be dismissed as a minor issue , only for it to turn into a full-blown infestation over time . Similarly , some homeowners may not be aware of the importance of maintaining proper hygiene and sealing entry points , which are essential steps in pest prevention . <p> Urban Density <p> The high population density in Dublin makes it easier for pests to spread rapidly from one location to another . Rodents and insects , in particular , can quickly move between properties , which makes it harder to eliminate infestations . <p> Resistance to Pesticides <p> Another challenge faced by pest control services is the increasing resistance of certain pests to conventional pesticides . Over time , pests such as rodents and insects can develop resistance to chemicals used to control them , making it more difficult to eradicate them effectively . <p> Addressing the Pest Infestation Problem in Dublin <p> As the demand for pest control grows in Dublin , both traditional and modern solutions are being utilised to effectively address pest problems . <p> Professional Pest Control Services <p> Many Dublin residents and businesses are turning to pest control companies to address growing infestations . Non-toxic pesticides , natural deterrents , and sustainable practices are becoming popular , reflecting broader environmental awareness in the city . <p> Regular Monitoring and Inspections <p> Regular inspections by pest control professionals are now a standard practice , particularly for businesses in the food and hospitality sectors . This ensures early detection of infestations and compliance with health regulations .

The second is that we are usually wrong -- or , if we do get it right , it is at least as likely to be the result of fortune as of brilliance . And the third is that all we can really do is to keep trying to make the new years better than the old ones .

Going over the cliff means entering a world where food , water , and weather systems - all the things we rely on for functioning civilisations - are severely disrupted . Yet no-one is pumping the brakes . <p> Global carbon emissions are going up and we are still waiting for the implementation of ambitious climate action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and stabilise global temperature . <p> So , it is a normal and appropriate response to be rightly worried about climate change , and taking tangible steps in 2025 to lessen our impact on the planet is a good way to deal with that anxiety . <p> I hate to break it to you , but bringing a reusable bag to the supermarket is not going to save the planet . This accelerating loss of ice is a critical indicator of the ongoing climate crisis . Glaciers , too , are disappearing at an alarming rate , with Switzerland 's glaciers losing up to 10% of their volume in just two years . <p> The WMO reports that global sea levels are rising at an unprecedented pace , more than double the rate observed in the late 20th century . <p> As the oceans warm , they expand , adding to the rising tide that threatens coastal cities and communities around the world . <p> Even if global temperatures stabilise at 2 ? C above pre-industrial levels , the rise in sea levels will persist , with projections indicating that millions of people living in vulnerable coastal areas may face displacement . <p> The consequences of this ongoing ice melt and rising seas are profound , with significant long-term implications for ecosystems , economies , and human populations . <p> In addition to the global impact , the largest recorded ice loss in history occurred in 2023 , further underscoring the urgency of addressing climate change . As the climate continues to warm , these health threats are exacerbated , especially in regions already struggling with inadequate healthcare systems . <p> In regions across Africa , Asia , and Latin America , communities are grappling with more frequent and severe climate-induced disasters , making it harder for vulnerable populations to recover and adapt . <p> The United Nations reports that millions have been displaced by flooding , droughts , and other climate-related crises , contributing to the global refugee crisis . <p> Kasim Yenigun , General manager of Desertification and Erosion Control at T ? rkiye 's Ministry of Environment , Urbanization , and Climate Change , highlighted how extreme events like floods and erosion are driving large-scale climate migrations , potentially surpassing other forms of displacement , mostly caused by wars or earthquakes . <p> Yenigun emphasised the importance of sustainable land management and combating desertification , referencing the " Ankara Initiative " launched in 2015 . <p> Of the 120 million forcibly displaced people worldwide , three-quarters live in countries heavily impacted by climate change . The failure to curb emissions remains a critical obstacle in combating climate change , and without decisive action , the future of the planet is increasingly uncertain . <p> According to the WMO , global efforts must intensify to meet the Paris Agreement targets . Hasar highlighted the transformative shift in energy , with renewables and electric vehicles leading the way . <p> Solar energy is a standout , with 599 GW of capacity added in 2024 , led by China , India , and the US . However , the pace of change is insufficient to avoid catastrophic impacts . <p> The UK has closed its last coal-fired power plant , while Norway is pushing for 100 percent electric vehicles by 2025 . <p> The International Renewable Energy Agency ( IRENA ) reported record high renewable energy capacity in 2023 , but much more is needed in developing nations for a just transition . <p> Yenigun added , " Taking action is a necessity for the well-being of future generations . " <p> There is still a long way to go , particularly in developing nations . A just transition to clean energy requires significant investment and support to ensure that no one is left behind . The future hinges on our collective ability to act now .

@@119483627 <h> Call for water rates to be considered by Stormont to help algae-hit Lough Neagh <p> The introduction of water rates in Northern Ireland could be the key to addressing crumbling waste water infrastructure and the impact on waterways , it has been suggested . <p> It comes as the Stormont Executive works to halt an environmental crisis at Lough Neagh where noxious blooms of blue-green algae have covered the surface of the water across the past two summers . <p> The lough is the largest freshwater lake by surface area in the UK and Ireland , supplies 40 per cent of Northern Ireland 's drinking water and sustains a major eel-fishing industry . <p> But it is facing a " perfect storm " of a crisis caused by pollution , nutrients , climate change and invasive species , according to Gerry Darby , manager of the Lough Neagh Partnership . <p> He praised the approach and actions taken so far by Agriculture , Environment and Rural Affairs Minister Andrew Muir but warned of wider problems that need a whole-of-Executive approach . <p> In an interview with the PA news agency , Mr Darby said the Lough Neagh Action Plan , and particularly the setting up of a stakeholder forum led by Mr Muir , was very positive and a first for a minister . <p> Blue-green algae on Lough Neagh in July 2024 ( Niall Carson/PA ) <p> He said 10 of the actions have already been implemented , including water inspectors and looking to the private sector for innovation , but it will take decades to start to see improvement . <p> " Is the nutrient level going to come down immediately , no it 's not , is the level of phosphorus going to come down , probably not , but at least you can now begin to look at setting targets , " Mr Darby said . <p> " It 's important to remember it 's not just farmers , there are a lot of nutrients coming in off the waste management processing units within NI Water and septic tanks -- we 're all contributing to it and other factors such as topography , there is only one river out of the lough , there is not great flow to flush it out . <p> " There is also climate change as well as invasive species in there . It all came together to create a perfect storm and at least the minister has engaged with many organisations to try and find solutions . <p> " It will be a long-term solution , nobody has ever suggested that the reduction of nutrients in Lough Neagh is going to happen overnight , it is estimated that it will take somewhere between 10 to 20 years before we 're beginning to see change . " <p> However Mr Darby said part of the problem is that people assume the blue-green algae is the only problem in the lough , pointing out the absence of a navigation authority as well as the waste water system which was described by the head of NI Water as being " at breaking point " . <p> He said addressing the waste water system will require the hard choice between trying to secure more money from the London government , rejigging the already strained Stormont budget or considering charging water rates . <p> While non-domestic water charges already apply in Northern Ireland , there has been strong political opposition to introducing domestic water charges . <p> " The other elephant in the room is the money needed for infrastructure for waste water management . This year the budget of NI Water for capital investment has been cut in half . That is a big , serious issue that politicians need to find an answer to , " Mr Darby said . <p> Blue-green algae on the River Bann where it meets Lough Neagh near the village of Toome , Co Antrim ( Niall Carson/PA ) <p> " There are three choices -- you ask Westminster to cough up more , Stormont reprioritises budgets , or else the big controversial one is that you introduce water rates , which is pretty standard in the rest of the UK . <p> " I could n't comment on that personally but I think it is something that needs to be given serious consideration to in the context of the issues also facing Belfast Lough .
